short: LIN54 is the DNA-binding subunit of the MuvB core, the module shared by the repressive DREAM complex and the activating MMB (B-MYB-MuvB) and FOXM1-MuvB complexes. It reads a very short promoter element called the CHR, the cell cycle genes homology region, whose consensus is TTYGAA (most often TTTGAA or TTCGAA). Recognition is unusual: two tandem cysteine-rich CXC (tesmin/CRC) domains grip the duplex and two tyrosine side chains insert into the minor groove, with no zinc finger or helix-turn-helix involved. The CHR is the reason so many G2/M promoters - CCNB1, CCNB2, CDK1, CDC25C, PLK1, AURKA, UBE2C - share the same short TTYGAA, switching from repressed in G0/G1 to activated in G2/M.
long:
## The factors

LIN54 (also called MIP120, and CXCD1) is one of five subunits of the MuvB core, together with LIN9,
LIN37, LIN52 and RBBP4. MuvB is the shared module of three complexes that act sequentially through the
cell cycle. In quiescence and early G1 it assembles with E2F4, DP1 and the RB-family pocket protein p130
(RBL2) to form DREAM, which represses. On entry into S phase p130 and E2F4 leave and B-MYB (MYBL2) binds,
giving MMB; later FOXM1 is recruited, giving FOXM1-MuvB, which activates the same promoters in G2 and M.
LIN54 is the only subunit with sequence-specific DNA-binding activity, so it supplies the address for all
three complexes. There is a single human LIN54 gene, so there is no paralogue ambiguity, and the protein
is broadly expressed in proliferating and quiescent cells alike. Its DNA-binding module is not a zinc
finger: it consists of two tandem cysteine-rich CXC domains, related to the tesmin/CRC domain family, and
both are required for high-affinity binding. The Drosophila orthologue Mip120 is part of the dREAM/MMB
complex with the same architecture.

## The motif

The CHR was defined genetically in 1995 as a short element in the CCNA2, CDC25C and CDK1 promoters, sitting
just downstream of a second element, the CDE, in a CDE-CHR tandem. The literature consensus is TTYGAA -
in practice TTTGAA or TTCGAA - and the atlas data agree: the JASPAR LIN54 model is TTTGAAT and the CIS-BP
model is ATTCAAA, which is the same element on the reverse strand. Family cohesion is 0.99, essentially
one motif in two orientations.

One genuine disagreement is worth flagging. The genome-wide survey by Engeland's group defined the
functional spectrum around TTYGAA, while the crystallographic study of LIN54 bound to DNA reported the
biochemically selected consensus as TTYRAA, which admits TTTAAA and TTCAAA as well. Both statements are
in the literature; the practical difference is whether a central G is required. The structure explains why
the information content is so low: specificity comes from two tyrosine residues inserting into the minor
groove rather than from major-groove base readout, a mode that reads a short AT-rich stretch with modest
discrimination. That tyrosine-mediated contact is required for MuvB recruitment to target promoters in
cells.

The element is 6 bp of low-complexity sequence. That is the single most important fact for reading a hit:
TTTGAA occurs roughly every few kilobases in random sequence.

## Where it acts

CHR elements are promoter elements, not enhancer elements, and they sit close to the transcription start
site, typically within about 20-100 bp downstream of it. They occur in most late (G2/M) cell-cycle genes
that bind DREAM, MMB or FOXM1-MuvB: CCNB1, CCNB2, CDK1, CDC25C, PLK1, AURKA, AURKB, BUB1, CENPF and UBE2C
among many others. Inverse-orientation CHRs are functional. Some promoters use a CDE-CHR tandem in which
an E2F4-contacted CDE enhances DREAM binding, and some use a CHR alone; the CHR, not the CDE, is the
element that is strictly required. By contrast, canonical MYB-binding and forkhead-binding sites are
under-represented in these promoters, even though B-MYB and FOXM1 act there - they arrive by protein
interaction with MuvB rather than by binding their own sites. The structural work also suggests MuvB
binding near the start site helps position downstream nucleosomes. The p53-p21-DREAM axis routes p53
signalling to these same CHR promoters, so CHR-containing G2/M genes are among the most reliably
p53-repressed genes in the genome.

## Biology and disease

The CHR is the mechanistic answer to a common observation: that G2/M genes behave as a tightly coordinated
module with almost identical expression timing. They share one element and one binding protein. Loss of
LIN54 or other MuvB subunits impairs mitotic gene expression and cell-cycle progression, and a LIN54
mutant in the CXC region mislocalizes to the cytoplasm and blocks the cycle. DREAM disruption
de-represses G2/M genes in quiescence, which is one route by which RB-pathway and p53-pathway lesions in
cancer produce the proliferation signature seen in tumour expression profiles. The CHR is therefore less
a disease gene than the promoter grammar through which two of the most commonly disrupted tumour
suppressor pathways act.

## Reading a hit

A CHR match tells you a G2/M cell-cycle promoter is plausible; it does not tell you that LIN54 is bound.
Six low-complexity bases match far too often for a single hit to be evidence. What raises confidence is
context, not score: the match should be in a promoter, within roughly 100 bp of the transcription start
site, in a gene whose expression peaks in G2/M, and ideally accompanied by a CDE a few bases away. Outside
that context, treat TTTGAA as background. There is no paralogue problem, because LIN54 is the only protein
known to read this element, but there is an interpretation problem in the other direction: because MuvB
carries B-MYB, FOXM1, E2F4 and p130 to the DNA, ChIP-seq for any of those factors will return CHR
elements without those factors binding DNA themselves, and a CHR hit under a FOXM1 or MYBL2 peak is
usually indirect. The CIS-BP LIN54 model is inferred from chicken LIN54 at 99% DNA-binding-domain
identity rather than measured on the human protein, and note the TTYGAA-versus-TTYRAA disagreement when
choosing how strict to be about the central base.
caveats: The CHR is 6 bp of low-complexity sequence (TTYGAA; TTTGAA and TTCGAA), so it matches frequently by chance and a single hit carries almost no information. Confidence comes from context: promoter location within roughly 100 bp of the transcription start site, a gene with G2/M-peaking expression, and often an adjacent CDE. Two consensus definitions coexist - TTYGAA from genome-wide promoter analysis and TTYRAA from in vitro selection with the LIN54 CXC domains - so whether a central G is required is unsettled. LIN54 is the only known reader, so there is no paralogue problem, but B-MYB, FOXM1, E2F4 and p130 all reach CHRs through MuvB, so their ChIP peaks contain CHRs indirectly. The CIS-BP model is inferred from chicken LIN54 (99% DBD identity).
